newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Students hold brief protest on E.Timor anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Students hold brief protest on E.Timor anniversary.

text.p: Students at the University of East Timor staged a brief protest in front of the campus on Tuesday on the fifth anniversary of the killing of at least 50 demonstrators by Indonesian troops in the capital Dili.
A university student said around noon that the situation at the campus was back to normal and there had been no trouble.

University officials had closed the university for the day but most students had turned up for classes as usual, and were left milling around the campus. Phone calls to the university were not answered.
A police official denied there was any problem, although residents said riot police were deployed in the streets around the university in the small, tropical sea-front city.
They said there was no sign of a confrontation between the several hundred students and police. A military compound is near the university, but there was no sign of troop movements.

Indonesian troops killed 50 demonstrators in 1991 following a funeral for an anti-Indonesian activist in Dili, according to an official report. Witnesses and human rights groups estimated at least 180 people died and many were injured.

In Jakarta, more than 2,000 members of the youth wing of Indonesia's ruling Golkar party paraded in front of parliament, calling for the expulsion of East Timorese Nobel Peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo from the country.

Newspaper reports said Belo was due to appear before a parliamentary commission on Tuesday to answer questions about an interview with the German news magazine Der Spiegel in which he was reported to have said Indonesian troops had trampled on East Timor's independence "and treated us like dogs".
Church sources said the Roman Catholic bishop had flown from the East Timor capital Dili on Monday and was attending an annual bishops' meeting in Jakarta.

Belo, jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize last month with self-exiled East Timorese-born anti-Indonesian activist Jose Ramos-Horta, has said he wanted to see the full text of the Der Spiegel interview before he commented further.

Regarded as probably the most influential civilian in East Timor and highly regarded by the territory's mainly-Catholic population, the bishop has called for an end to demonstrations and violence there.
Youths dressed in yellow uniforms carried banners proclaiming "Expel Belo", and "Thank you Malaysian government" as they walked in front of parliament.

The Malaysian government condemned an abortive weekend Asian-Pacific conference on East Timor by activists critical of Indonesia, saying the gathering could damage Malaysia's relations with neighbouring Indonesia.
Youths allied to Malaysia's ruling coalition broke up the conference in a Kuala Lumpur hotel on Saturday and Malaysia subsequently deported foreign participants.
Sources in close contact with East Timor said Tuesday's demonstration at the university was apparently connected to an article attacking Belo published in an Indonesian newspaper last week.
The article in the Suara Timor Timur (Voice of East Timor) newspaper angered the students, who demanded an apology from the Indonesian paper.

The sources said there had also been a heated dialogue on Monday between students and members of the official National Commission on Human Rights. Because of tension evident at the meeting, the rector closed the university on Tuesday.
